# Learning with Alternating Moduli, Arora-Ge over Composite Moduli, and Weak PRFs

##### Chen, Y.; Ji, L.; Li, W.

* * *

#### Lecture Notes in Computer Science 16802 LNCS: 201-231

#### 2026

* * *

ISSN/ISBN: 0302-9743

DOI: 10.1007/978-3-032-35377-1_7
Accession: 110190808


##### Summary

In TCC 2018, Boneh, Ishai, Passelègue, Sahai, and Wu propose candidates of weak and strong PRFs by evaluating linear functions over coprime moduli alternatively. Such PRFs can be evaluated by low-depth circuits and are MPC-friendly. However, they have not been able to base the security of their PRFs on well-formed assumptions other than assuming that the PRF constructions themselves are secure. In this paper, we formalize a new assumption called Learning with Alternating Moduli (LAM). We show that over certain large moduli, the LAM assumption is as hard as the Learning with Errors (LWE) assumption. For LAM over constant moduli, we do not know how to base its hardness on the LWE assumption. Instead, we provide polynomial-time attacks on LAM with constant prime-power moduli and certain constant non-prime-power moduli, andevidence of the sub-exponential hardness of LAM with other moduli by analyzing the effect of typical attacks. polynomial-time attacks on LAM with constant prime-power moduli and certain constant non-prime-power moduli, and evidence of the sub-exponential hardness of LAM with other moduli by analyzing the effect of typical attacks. More specifically, we put forward two new attacks. The first attack is a recursive algorithm that solves LWE with certain constant composite moduli and error distributions. The algorithm extends the Arora-Ge algorithm for LWE from prime moduli to composite moduli, and it also solves LAM for certain parameters. The second attack is a polynomial-time attack that rules out the existence of weak PRFs in NC0[p] for any prime p. Based on our studies, we propose candidate weak PRFs in NC0[p1,p2] for some distinct primes p1,p2 based on LAM over constant moduli, or the Learning with Rounding (LWR) assumption over constant moduli. Compared to the weak PRF candidates by Boneh et al., our weak PRF candidates live in the same complexity class while having the advantage of being based on well-formed assumptions.

L39: 【20†learning parities with noise】, 【21†learning with errors】, 【22†linearization】
L40: 
L41: Abstract:
L42: 
L43: We give new algorithms for a variety of randomly-generated instances of computational problems using a linearization technique that reduces to solving a system of linear equations.
L44: These algorithms are derived in the context of learning with structured noise, a notion introduced in this paper. This notion is best illustrated with the learning parities with noise (LPN) problem ---well-studied in learning theory and cryptography. In the standard version, we have access to an oracle that, each time we press a button, returns a random vector $ a \in GF(2)^n$ together with a bit $b \in GF(2)$ that was computed as
L45: $a\cdot u +\eta$, where $u\in GF(2)^n$ is a secret vector, and $\eta \in GF(2)$ is a noise bit that is $1$ with some probability $p$. Say $p=1/3$. The goal is to recover $u$. This task is conjectured to be intractable.
L46: In the structured noise setting we introduce a slight (?) variation of the model: upon pressing a button, we receive (say) $10$ random vectors
L47: $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{10} \in GF(2)^n$, and corresponding bits $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{10}$, of which at most $3$ are noisy. The oracle may arbitrarily decide which of the $10$ bits to make noisy. We exhibit a polynomial-time algorithm to recover the secret vector $u$ given such an oracle. We think this structured noise model may be of independent interest in machine learning.
L48: We discuss generalizations of our result, including learning with more general noise patterns. We also give the first nontrivial algorithms
L49: for two problems, which we show fit in our structured noise framework.
L50: 
L51: We give a slightly subexponential algorithm for the well-known learning with errors (LWE) problem over $GF(q)$ introduced by Regev for cryptographic uses. Our algorithm works for the case when the gaussian noise is small; which was an open problem.
L52: We also give polynomial-time algorithms for learning the MAJORITY OF PARITIES function of Applebaum et al. for certain parameter
L53: values. This function is a special case of Goldreich's pseudorandom generator.

L65: 【24†Lattice-based cryptography】, 【25†learning decision trees】, 【20†learning parities with noise】, 【21†learning with errors】, 【22†linearization】
L66: 
L67: Abstract:
L68: In the {\em learning parities with noise} problem ---well-studied in learning theory and cryptography--- we
L69: have access to an oracle that, each time we press a button,
L70: returns a random vector $ a \in \GF(2)^n$ together with a bit $b \in \GF(2)$ that was computed as
L71: $a\cdot u +\eta$, where $u\in \GF(2)^n$ is a {\em secret} vector, and $\eta \in \GF(2)$ is a {\em noise} bit
L72: that is $1$ with some probability $p$. Say $p=1/3$. The goal is to recover $u$. This task is
L73: conjectured to be intractable.
L74: Here we introduce a slight (?) variation of the model: upon pressing a button, we receive (say) $10$ random vectors
L75: $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{10} \in \GF(2)^n$, and corresponding bits $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{10}$, of which at most $3$ are
L76: noisy. The oracle may arbitrarily decide which of the $10$ bits to make noisy.
L77: We exhibit a polynomial-time algorithm to recover the secret vector $u$ given such an oracle.
L78: We discuss generalizations of our result, including learning with more general noise patterns.
L79: We can also learn
L80: low-depth decision trees in the above structured noise model. We also consider the {\em learning with errors} problem
L81: over $\GF(q)$ and give (a) a $2^{\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})}$ algorithm in our structured noise setting (b) a slightly subexponential algorithm when the gaussian noise is small.
